title: Searching: Finding Your Name in the Register
learningGoals: write a linear search that returns the index or -1
explain how binary search halves the range with low, mid and high
write a correct binary search loop
know that binary search only works on a sorted array

youtube.title: Linear vs Binary Search in C, Explained | EP 43
youtube.description: How do you find one roll number among a thousand? Check every name, or cut the register in half again and again. Learn linear search and binary search in C, step by step, and why binary search gives wrong answers on unsorted data. 0:00 The register · 0:20 Title · 0:25 Linear search · 1:05 Linear code · 2:05 Binary search idea · 3:05 Binary code · 4:50 Running it · 5:10 How fast? · 5:30 Pun · 5:35 Bug of the Day · 6:25 Challenge · 6:50 Next episode

thumbnail.visual: big text "FIND IT IN 10 STEPS"; a stack of 1000 roll-number cards being cut in half by a giant claw; Xecxec smug with arms crossed; dark-blue "mid" arrow

scenes.animation: Pages flip fast; Xecxec yawning with a finger running down the page; page-flip SFX
scenes.narration: The teacher hands you the attendance register and says, find roll number 26. You start at the top and go one by one. That works. But imagine the register had a thousand names. There is a smarter way, and by the end of this video your program will find any name in a thousand in about ten steps.

scenes.onScreen: Eight boxes 3 8 12 17 21 26 30 35; checker moves left to right
scenes.animation: Current box in butter, match turns mint; tick per check, ding on match
scenes.narration: The simple way is called linear search. Linear means in a line. Start at the first box. Is it 26? No. Next box. No. Keep going until you find it, or until you run out of boxes. Here, 26 sits at index five, so we checked six boxes. If the value is not there at all, we check every single box before we can say "not found".

scenes.animation: Line highlights; tracker shows i, found
scenes.narration: Here is the code. [HL 4] Line four: eight roll numbers. [HL 6] Line six: target is the number we want, 26. [HL 9] Line nine: found starts at minus one. Minus one can never be a real index, so it is our signal for "not found yet". [TRACK found=-1] [HL 10] Line ten, the usual loop over every index. [HL 11] Line eleven: if rolls i equals target, [TRACK i=5] [HL 12] save the index in found, [TRACK found=5] [HL 13] and break, from EP 29, to stop the loop early. No need to keep looking once we have it. [HL 16] Line sixteen prints the result: index five. Simple, and it works on any array, sorted or not.

code.output:
Linear: found at index 5
Binary: found at index 5

scenes.onScreen: Same eight boxes; low, mid, high arrows; half greys out each step
scenes.animation: Grey-out sweep; snip SFX per halving
scenes.narration: Now the smart way. Notice our roll numbers are sorted, smallest to largest. That is the key. Binary search looks at the middle box first. low is the first index, zero. high is the last, seven. mid is zero plus seven, divided by two, which is three in integer division. rolls three is 17. Is 26 bigger than 17? Yes. So 26 cannot be anywhere on the left half. Throw that half away. Now low becomes four. New mid is four plus seven by two, five. rolls five is 26. Found it, in two steps instead of six. Every step cuts the remaining boxes in half. It is like the Kadamba bus conductor who knows the stops are in order: if you say Panjim, he does not check every seat; he knows exactly which half of the route you belong to.

scenes.animation: Line highlights; tracker shows low, high, mid, pos
scenes.narration: Let's read it. [HL 19] Line nineteen sets up three variables. low equals zero, high equals n minus one, and pos equals minus one for "not found". [TRACK low=0 high=7 pos=-1] [HL 20] Line twenty: while low is less than or equal to high. As long as there is at least one box left to check, keep going. [HL 21] Line twenty-one finds the middle. [TRACK mid=3] [HL 22] Line twenty-two: if the middle value is our target, [HL 23] save it and break. [HL 25] Line twenty-five: else if the middle value is smaller than the target, the target must be on the right side. [HL 26] So low becomes mid plus one. [TRACK low=4] Plus one, because we already checked mid. [HL 27] Otherwise, the middle value is bigger, the target is on the left, [HL 28] and high becomes mid minus one. [TRACK mid=5 pos=5] Back to the top of the loop, new mid is five, rolls five is 26, pos becomes five, and we break. [HL 31] Line thirty-one prints the answer. And if the target is not there at all, low and high cross over, the loop ends, and pos stays minus one.

code.output:

Binary: found at index 5

scenes.narration: Compile and run. Linear: found at index five. Binary: found at index five. Same answer, but binary took two steps, linear took six.

scenes.onScreen: Steps for 1,000 items: linear up to 1000, binary about 10
scenes.animation: Two counters race; binary finishes in a blink; whoosh
scenes.narration: With a thousand sorted items, linear search may need a thousand checks. Binary search needs about ten, because halving a thousand ten times gets you down to one. With a million items, binary search needs about twenty. That is why it is one of the most famous ideas in computer science.
Why is binary search so calm? It never gets more than half worried.

scenes.onScreen: Binary search on an unsorted array returns -1 for a value that is there
scenes.animation: Boxes shuffled; arrows skip right past 21; alarm buzz
scenes.narration: Today's bug. Same binary search code, but the array is not sorted: 21, 3, 35, 12, 30, 8, 26, 17. We search for 21. It is right there at index zero. Compile, no errors. Run it. Binary: found at index minus one. Not found! Here is why. mid is three, the value is 12. 21 is bigger, so binary search throws away the left half, including index zero, where 21 actually was. Binary search trusts that the array is sorted. If it is not, it throws away the wrong half. The fix: sort the array first, or use linear search. And how do we sort? That is next episode.

scenes.onScreen: Search a roll number typed by the user
scenes.narration: Your challenge. Use the sorted roll numbers. Ask the user to type a roll number with scanf. Use binary search to find it. If found, print "Roll 30 is at position 7", where position is the index plus one. If not found, print "Roll 9 is not in the class".

scenes.animation: Xecxec lining up shells by size; sign-off
scenes.narration: Next episode: why order matters, and how to swap two values. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
No error, no warning. Wrong output (21 is at index 0):

Binary: found at index -1
bug.why: binary search throws away half the array based on the middle value, which is only safe when every value on the left is smaller and every value on the right is bigger.

shorts.title: 1000 Names, 10 Steps
shorts.hook: Giant register: "Find one name in 1000. In 10 steps."
shorts.script: Find one name in a thousand, in about ten steps. Impossible? Not if the list is sorted. Look at the middle. Too small? Throw away the left half. Too big? Throw away the right half. Repeat. That is binary search.
shorts.caption: The trick behind every fast search.

shorts.title: Binary Search in 30 Seconds
shorts.hook: low, mid, high arrows over eight boxes.
shorts.script: Three arrows: low, mid, high. mid is low plus high, divided by two. If the middle value is your target, done. If it is smaller, move low to mid plus one. If it is bigger, move high to mid minus one. Keep going while low is less than or equal to high.
shorts.caption: Binary search, the whole idea.

shorts.title: It's Right There!
shorts.hook: Terminal: "found at index -1" with 21 glowing at index 0.
shorts.script: 21 is right there at index zero, but binary search says not found. Why? The array is not sorted. The middle value was 12, 21 is bigger, so it threw away the left half, the half that had 21. Binary search only works on sorted data.
shorts.caption: Binary search has one rule. Break it and it lies.

shorts.title: Half Worried
shorts.hook: Xecxec meditating on a split coconut half.
shorts.script: Why is binary search so calm? It never gets more than half worried.
shorts.caption: Stay calm, cut in half.

shorts.title: How Many Steps?
shorts.hook: "1,000,000 sorted items. Binary search needs how many steps?"
shorts.script: A million sorted items. How many steps does binary search need? Pause and guess. About twenty. Each step halves the list, and halving a million about twenty times leaves one item. Linear search could need a million.
shorts.caption: Halving is a superpower.
